bodyEn: Valdas Dambrauskas can reel off the questions and answers without a moment’s pause. Who won the first Academy Award for best actor in 1929? It was Emil Jannings, even if someone else might have been tempted to go with Charlie Chaplin. Which country publishes the highest number of daily newspapers? India was the clear winner. Can you name the nation that produces the most electricity per capita in the world? His family, watching back home, clasped heads in hands but he was right: back then, in 2002, the answer was his native Lithuania.

It was enough to win Dambrauskas about £725 in his appearance on Six Zeros – A Million, the Lithuanian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? “At that time it was quite big money,” he says. “I could have bought a flat in my home town; it was a very difficult period there and they were almost free. But my plan was to go to England and follow my dream to become a coach, and that’s how it started.”

More than two and a half decades later the story continues at Old Trafford where Dambrauskas will manage the Azerbaijani champions, Sabah, in their Champions League debut on Thursday night. The club’s journey is some tale in itself given Sabah, who came through a dramatic playoff with Hapoel Be’er Sheva, did not exist until 2017. But the path taken by their head coach, a 25-year-old office worker with only a modest football background when his general knowledge skills were put on display, is virtually unparalleled in the modern game.

The money he won helped Dambrauskas and his girlfriend, now wife, to move to north London and establish themselves in an alien environment. “I would have done it anyway – the show came in the middle of our planning,” he says of the move, which became an ambition after a work visit to Norway in 2000.

In Scandinavia he had grasped the extent of the Premier League’s incipient popularity. “I realised this was where real football is. There was no pathway to coaching in Lithuania if you hadn’t been a player; it was impossible. But if I could take a course in England, maybe I could get a chance to step on the ladder at home.”

Dambrauskas spent eight years in London. “The start was very, very difficult. I wasn’t speaking decent English, had no contacts, we didn’t know anyone, we lived in different places, did all kinds of jobs.” He worked in a Muswell Hill pub, delivered newspapers in the area, held down jobs in a nursery school, as a gardener, in sales, and as a self-employed handyman, often simultaneously. The hours were relentless but so was the young man’s focus.

It was a life of an immigrant couple straining every sinew to make their way. Their first child was born in 2004; by then Dambrauskas, who had studied philosophy and social sciences in Lithuania, had enrolled on a sports science and coaching course at London Metropolitan University. From his classroom on the 10th floor he could see the Emirates Stadium sprouting up during that spell of Arsenal invincibility.

The Access to Sports Project, based in Finsbury Park, is a stone’s throw from Arsenal but galaxies away in another sense. It is where Dambrauskas landed his first coaching role, giving sessions to children on Saturday mornings and during school holidays. His next step is all the more remarkable for what has passed since. A round of interviews with Manchester United Soccer Schools brought the chance to work with youngsters around the country, and sometimes on residential trips abroad, under the banner of the then serial title winners. Despite the name it was a far cry from even academy football, but the injection of confidence was transformative.

“It was John Shiels, CEO of the Manchester United Foundation, who gave me the chance. I don’t know what he saw in me – I came in with very broken English and couldn’t express myself as I can now – but he really supported me. At the end of the year he wrote me an appraisal of what I’d done. He said that I was good and could do much more. It was a massive, massive boost for me.”

Through a friend at university, Dambrauskas became involved with the community sports organisation London Tigers. “He told me they always needed coaches.” Eventually he took charge of their semi-professional team, which played in the Spartan South Midlands League. “That was where it really started, coaching at some kind of level.” It meant managing in the FA Vase and the early rounds of the FA Cup.

Dambrauskas also undertook part-time roles at Fulham and Brentford before working as a sports activator for Central YMCA on Tottenham Court Road. He would later take a broader role as sports development manager at London Tigers and took his coaching badges at the London Football Association. “It was a time with no holidays, no days off. I’m a big reader, I read all the time and studied constantly. Sometimes I would finish my university work on the bus. I took every kind of education I could and went to every possible course for every meeting.

“Over the years I had countless interviews for coaching roles, for jobs at centres of excellency in London and outside, so many CVs and applications, but I understood early on that it’s very difficult in England to get on the ladder and that to coach at professional level there was probably impossible. If there is a story where someone is starting in the community scheme and going all the way to become a head coach, I am still to find it.”

By late 2010 he felt ready to pursue what had originally been the end goal: a role in Lithuania. He had started working with their under-17s and agreed to join Ekranas, national champions at the time, as assistant manager. “I had the London Tigers job, 15 hours a week at Brentford and some other things here and there. We had a good life and people thought I was crazy going back home and earning about a fifth of what I was getting in England. But the biggest risk in life is not to take risks.

“I’m forever grateful to my wife for being behind me. We always faced questions: twenty- or thirtysomething guy always studying, trying to work in football, spending all his money on books and courses rather than buying an apartment or something for the family. But I’m very happy with how it turned out and nobody questions those decisions now.”

A kaleidoscopic career bloomed. By December 2014 he had become head coach at Zalgiris Vilnius, the biggest club in Lithuania, winning two more league titles and various cups in a move that felt unthinkable during a humble upbringing in the tiny northern town Pakruojis. “My childhood was not a gift. My dad died when I was 11, and if he knew that I had the job at Zalgiris and that we won so many trophies he would be the happiest person in the world.”

Dambrauskas was not content to stop there. “You are basically nobody and suddenly you get this job. Then you have to prove yourself to everybody again and again and again. So you reached this step on the ladder but what’s next? How do you go to the next level?”

After three years he joined the upwardly mobile Latvian club RFS but harboured concerns about the prospects of leaving the small Baltic football bubble. In the event he need not have worried. Since 2020 he has managed in Croatia with Gorica and Hajduk Split – the latter are “like a tattoo you can’t ever take out, it leaves a mark on you” – in Bulgaria with Ludogorets, in Greece with OFI Crete, in Cyprus with Omonia and with the Hungarian club Diosgyor, who he describes as having “one of the biggest hidden football potentials in Europe”.

Itinerant career paths such as that are, especially in eastern and southern Europe, nothing new. But Sabah had been courting Dambrauskas for two years before he took over in 2025. Once the stars had aligned, he worked a miracle. In 2024-25, Sabah had finished 41 points behind the biggest club in Azerbaijan, Qarabag. Last season Sabah beat them to the title by nine points, earning their crack at the Champions League qualifiers. “I’m really grateful to Qarabag. Every game against them is like taking a master’s degree.”

He waxes lyrical about the stability and facilities available at well-backed Sabah, who were cheered on with fervour befitting a national team when they thrillingly overcame an injury-time deficit against Be’er Sheva. Their success has come with a multinational squad that plays bold, front-foot football in the style he preaches. “But if you don’t understand the human being in front of you, it’s very difficult to pass him your ideas and build trust,” he says.

“What is important in east Africa can be completely different from what someone needs in west Africa or anywhere across Europe. You need to be able to understand different cultures, different traditions, different ways of speaking or behaving. Without that it’s impossible to do anything, and I believe this is where my strength lies.”

It is a glorious piece of circularity that Dambrauskas and Sabah will be watched from the stands on Thursday by a number of his old colleagues from Manchester United Soccer Schools. He beams at the thought; none of this could have seemed remotely attainable during their time on the grass together. “But I had this belief. I had this confidence all the time that I could do it.”

He is equally delighted that the draw has also brought a January visit to Arsenal, that huge presence in his eyeline during those years studying on Holloway Road. He is 49 and would surely lever himself among Europe’s most sought-after coaching properties if he can take Sabah further. “We’re going to respect everyone but not be afraid of anyone. There’s a very nice song by the Lithuanian band Colours of Bubbles called Truth or Dare. Very soon we’re going to find out the truth about ourselves and what we can do. It will be very beneficial for us because I don’t want this club to be a one-day wonder.” As final answers go, it may be his most significant yet.

items.titleEn: Every word: Arteta's post-Napoli press conference
items.summaryEn: Find out what the manager had to say to the media in Naples following our Champions League opener
bodyEn: After seeing his side put in a tremendous effort to beat Napoli 1-0 and start the Champions League league phase with a win, Mikel Arteta answered questions from the media.
He spoke about the chances created, the performance of his captain, our incredible form in Europe and much more. Here is everything he had to say:

on the result:Very, very happy, the way we attacked the game from the very first minute, the way we competed, the excitement that we had, how we had to attack them, how we had to disorganise them, the purpose, the quality, the amount of chances that we generated. For sure, again, the scoreline has to reflect a very different result. We will get there, because if we are a bit more precise, it will be much bigger, but to do what we've done today in this stadium against this opponent is remarkable from the team.
on being more clinical in front of goal:

When you talk about people being clinical, the reality is that they score one in every five or six shots on target. That's being clinical. So, if we generate more volume, we will score more goals. The number of players that got into this situation, the amount of situations that we were generating in various ways was something that pleased me a lot, and the fact that obviously it's 1-0 at the end. To suffer, they had that situation with Kevin [De Bruyne] inside the box, that any other day something different could have happened, but I'm really pleased, because we won the game, and I think we fully deserved to win.

on Martin Odegaard’s match-winning performance:That's what we need, the players with that mindset to decide the game, and to play with that personality, that an action might not happen, it's the next one, the next one, and keep insisting, keep taking chances and risks. He's getting into those positions much more in recent games, and now you feel he has this emotional state that he knows that the ball can go in, and he scored an incredible goal tonight.

on if he’s been asked to get into attacking positions more:Yes, because he can, and we have now a lot of players that can take the ball there and they can progress the ball much better than we did in the past. When that happens he needs to take different heights and angles and positions in order to disorganise the opponent, and he's done that really well tonight.
on if he has set Martin a goals target:Yes, goals every week, every game goals, that's the target.

on us never giving up:Playing to the players' qualities and try to understand whether the opponent can have certain weaknesses or misjudgements and try to exploit them time after time, and again against a team that is so well-organised that they play in such short distances. It's complicated but it's very much doable because of the quality of the players that we have.

on our 13 league stage victories in a row:I think the hunger and desire of the team, and then each individual just putting his very best in every game, in every action, it's just a joy to watch. Every time we do it again, the way the team reacts, every time we have to try it back, even if it's a frustrating giveaway, it's just incredible. That's what's going to give us the opportunity to do what we want to win, and to win this kind of game, to be so good at doing these kinds of things.

on if he sees Martin as a different man this season:First of all, he needs to be available, and last year he missed so many games through injuries. He's got that edge, and he's got now different relationships around him as well, and that helps, and now he can start to occupy some very different heights in the team, especially in the attacking phase, and when we get him into those positions, he’s a very dangerous player.

on how we dealt with Rasmus Hojlund’s pace:That's the risk, but that also means that if I'm a free man in defence, I'll have one more player on the pitch. Against a low block like that, we have to take that risk. We have defenders who can solve this situation - it's true that it's one or two situations on the pitch today that we've had a bit of luck, but that's something we run the risk of because we want to be dominant, and without that it's not easy.

on if he expected this type of Napoli performance:I expected it, I wanted it, but it was very similar to the one that we played. There are a lot of circumstances that allow you to play this game or not. If there is a player in Napoli that is one of my favourite-ever players, that is Kevin De Bruyne, who I had the luxury to train and to be with him for almost four years. In my opinion, he is one of the best midfielders ever and still a joy to watch him play.

items.titleEn: Rice on how we beat the heat to score a fine winner
items.summaryEn: Declan Rice reveals the mood in the camp following our Champions League victory at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona
bodyEn: After he and his teammates all played their part in creating the goal that beat Napoli, Declan Rice praised our ability to play top-drawer football in tough conditions.
With southern Italy basking in a heatwave, a 9pm kick-off began amidst temperatures pushing 30 degrees, and the humid, sticky conditions took their toll on both sets of players.

But when it mattered most, we produced a slick 29-pass move to finally carve open the home defence, finished by a superb Martin Odegaard strike that kissed the post on its way into the net to ensure our quest to reach the Champions League final again and right last season’s wrongs began in the best possible fashion.

“In my opinion, it could’ve been four or five tonight if we were a bit more clinical,” Rice mused post-match. “It’s rare you get that many chances inside the six-yard box, so we can improve on that front, but to generate those chances, the way we played, rotated, played with fluidity.

“The goal - it was just incredible. Everyone getting on [the ball], touching it, pass and move, pass and move to open them up. We were probing all game up until that point, so to score that - Martin again- so happy for him, a massive goal and a big three points.

“That’s probably the hottest game I’ve played in for Arsenal so far. It’s actually like how it was at the World Cup - humid, the pitch was dry, heavy as well, so it makes it tougher, but to still play the way we did and perform the way we did, everyone looked really strong and really fit.”

As well as the weather conditions, we also had to visit a venue that is traditionally a fortress for the Azzurri, who had never previously lost two consecutive European games on their turf. But that has now happened after we added the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona to our ever-growing list of iconic stadia across the continent we have won at, helping to build confidence ahead of trips to Bayern Munich, Slavia Prague and Real Betis.

“I feel really lucky and blessed to play against these big historic teams,” Declan added. “We know what stadium this is and to play here is a massive honour. We’ve got some really big away games coming up in the Champions League we need to look forward to, we can’t take anything for granted and we keep pushing.

“Momentum is key. Football is really good when you’re winning matches, there’s no better feeling. Let’s keep momentum going, keep doing everything right, and just keep pushing. It’s still so early in the season, and to have that momentum and keep winning games is key for us, we want to keep doing it.”
Declan was also delighted for his captain, with Martin continuing his purple patch in front of goal this season by adding a fourth strike to his name in 2026/27.

After seeing him struggle last season with injury to ultimately guide us to the Premier League title, the England international is thrilled that his midfield partner in crime is reaping the rewards himself once again, and is determined to do what it takes to keep that going.

“He’s always had the ability - just last year, he was so unlucky with his injuries - so unlucky to have two shoulder injuries, an MCL, knee issues,” he added. “But when a player like that is fit and has that quality to play, he can shine in any team and for us he’s so important.

“For him to score three goals in the season so far, it’s massive for him but also unreal for us, because when he’s at the top of his game he makes us a better team. So let’s keep making him feel confident, giving him the ball and letting him do what he does best.”

items.titleEn: Arteta's delight with "immense" effort to beat Napoli
items.summaryEn: Get Mikel Arteta's thoughts as we began our Champions League campaign with a test in Naples
bodyEn: Mikel Arteta was delighted to kick-start another Champions League campaign with a big away win as Martin Odegaard’s goal beat Napoli in southern Italy.

While the scoreline will show another famous “1-0 to The Arsenal” victory, the margin of victory could have been much bigger, and the 24 shots we registered are the highest total we’ve hit in a Champions League away match on record.

To have done that at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona against a side that finished second in Serie A last season and had previously never lost consecutive home matches in Europe, is a feat that Mikel was delighted with, especially given the calmness and maturity we showed to stick with the gameplan and not panic when chances went begging.
“I'm very, very happy,” he said. “A really tough place to come and a really different environment to play football - a beautiful one, by the way - against a really good team.

“I love the way we attacked the game, the way we competed, the hunger that we showed, the desire to dominate, to come here, to own the pitch, and the quality that we showed against a team that it’s so difficult to create chances against. We created a huge amount of them and the result doesn't reflect what we saw on the pitch.
“The players were immense, and to play with that personality, with that conviction and with that quality in the Champions League away from home, it's something that I'm extremely pleased about.”

Odegaard popped up with the all-important winner, brilliantly finishing a fine 29-pass move on the edge of the box to score his fourth goal of the season already in just five outings. As well as scoring, he also created the most chances, had the most touches and made the most passes that broke the defensive line.
The skipper is on top of his game right now, and Mikel feels he's not only benefiting, but his teammates are also thriving by linking up with him on the pitch as he continues to lead by example.

“I think you can sense the momentum of the team, the flow,” Mikel suggested when asked about his captain’s influence. “When a player makes a mistake in the next section and takes the risk and he goes again. I think we were like a hammer today, just going and going and going until we broke them down.”

As well as starting with three points, the boss was also delighted to pick up our 13th successive win in the league phase of the competition for our travelling supporters, who suffered massive travel delays and issues due to air traffic control problems departing the UK.

“I think they put a huge effort, so thank you so much,” the boss added. “A huge gratitude to them to be here. It was tough yesterday; we were just thinking about them. We found a way to be here, a bit later than expected, but to be here, so from all of the club, a huge thank you and I hope they enjoy their victory.”

bodyEn: Raphinha let his goals do the talking after being omitted from the Ballon d’Or shortlist, striking twice as Barcelona eased to a 5-1 win over Feyenoord in the Champions League.

The Brazilian was a surprise omission from this week’s 30-strong list of candidates for the prestigious award but brushed any disappointment aside to continue his early season hot streak at a rain-soaked Camp Nou. The forward finished brilliantly in the third minute and added a second just before the hour mark to down the Eredivisie side and take his tally to eight goals in six outings at the start of the campaign.

The summer signing Karim Adeyemi produced a stunning finish, Lamine Yamal stroked a free-kick through a gap in the Dutch wall and recent arrival Gabriel Jesus opened his account for the club just two minutes after stepping off the bench.
There was little to celebrate for Giovanni van Bronckhorst on his Barça return but Sem Steijn gave the visiting fans something to enjoy when he poked in at far post late on.

“The most important thing is we are playing like a team, like one unit,” the Barcelona head coach, Hansi Flick, said. “We controlled the game, we are dominant and this is fantastic to see. This is our style and how we want to play.”

Ferran Torres scored a hat-trick and Ousmane Dembélé also starred as Paris Saint-Germain began their quest to win a third successive Champions League title by thrashing Slovan Bratislava 6-1 at the Parc des Princes.

Last year’s Ballon d’Or winner Dembélé had scored twice by the midway point of the first half in the French capital, and then set up Spain’s World Cup final hero Torres to make it 3-0 by the interval.

Torres, a close-season signing from Barcelona, added two more just after the restart to complete his hat-trick before the hour mark, with Suleiman Camara pulling one back for the Slovakian champions and Fabián Ruiz then sealing PSG’s win.
Elsewhere, Stuttgart’s Ermedin Demirovic struck a 12-minute first-half hat-trick to ⁠earn ⁠a ​3-1 victory over Viking Stavanger.

He opened the ​scoring after 20 minutes with a touch at the near post, but Viking, making their first appearance in the league phase of the Champions League, were level two minutes later when Zlatko Tripic finished a ⁠swift counter-attack with his left foot.

Demirovic quickly re-established the lead ​in the ​26th minute and then completed ​the hat-trick with a hooked volley six minutes later. “For me personally it was the perfect start and also for the team as a whole,” Demirovic told Dazn.

West Bromwich Albion held on for a memorable 1-0 victory over Derby at Pride Park, after playing for more than an hour with 10 men. Aune Heggebø's early goal proved enough to take the Baggies top of the table, despite Brayann Pereira being dismissed on his debut after collecting two first-half yellow cards.

Derby had started the stronger, but West Brom swept downfield to score in the 16th minute, Jimmy-Jay Morgan whipping in a low cross from the left which Heggebø [pictured] finished at the near post. The visitors were rocked by the dismissal of Pereira in the 34th minute, as he was shown a second yellow card for a clumsy challenge on Charlie Taylor.

The hosts went close just before half-time when David Ozoh flashed a low ball across the six-yard box with no white shirt able to turn it in. Derby should have levelled in the 68th minute but Lars-Jørgen Salvesen headed over from Joe Ward’s cross. Late on, Nat Phillips made a great clearance after a late goalmouth scramble, summing up a performance full of grit and resolve.

James Morrison's side move above West Ham to top the Championship table with 13 points from six games. Either Charlton or QPR could have joined them on 13 points, but the sides played out a stalemate at the Valley. Derby, meanwhile, slipped into the bottom three with their fourth defeat in six games.

Norwich moved up to ninth in the table as they edged past visitors Birmingham 2-1 to make it three wins in four league games. Oscar Schwartau's screamer opened the scoring, the young Dane lashing an unstoppable right-footed drive past James Beadle from 25 yards out.

Papa Diallo's first goal for the Canaries doubled their advantage before the break, as the Senegal winger sidefooted home from Andre Brooks' cross. Carlos Vicente pulled a goal back for the visitors, but wasted a glorious chance to equalise near the end as Chris Davies’ men suffered their first league defeat this season. Press Association
Sporting, quarter-finalists last season for the first time since 1983, fought back to see off Galatasaray 3-1 in Lisbon.

Galatasaray took an early lead through Gonçalo Inacio’s own goal but Geny ​Catamo punished poor defending to equalise in the 27th minute. Luis Suárez converted a 57th-minute penalty to put Sporting ahead and a blistering free kick from Rodrigo Zalazar six minutes later sealed the win.

items.summaryEn: Martin Ødegaard’s goal proved enough for Arsenal to start their campaign with three points2 min: Arsenal are wearing red shorts. Full marks for considering those with colour blindness, and acting with compassion. It doesn’t look good, mind. It’s just not Arsenal.After a moment to remember the victims of the devastating floods in Nepal, Arsenal get the ball rolling. A blistering atmosphere at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona; did anyone expect anything else? Continue reading...
bodyEn: Ed Aarons was in Naples tonight. Here’s his report. Thanks for reading this MBM!

Mikel Arteta – who is unsurprisingly cutting a much more relaxed figure this season – speaks to TNT. “A fully deserved three points … the amount of chances and situations we generated … that doesn’t reflect the result … it should have been a much bigger win … a really tough environment and opponent … the team was superb … attitude … courage … quality … it was a shame we missed so many big chances.”

Post-match postbag. “It’s going to be a tough season for Napoli as their only purchase seems to have been Favasuli from lowly Catanzaro whereas Arsenal have strengthened an already very powerful squad with the likes of Tsolis and Konsa. Essentially, Napoli played for pride and gave a fairly good account of themselves” – Colum Fordham
“Not Viktor’s biggest fan, but the failure of the other players to pass to him this evening - when he’s been in a perfect position to pull the trigger - has been an embarrassment” – Paul G
“I am still irked by the red shorts. Why aren’t Arsenal wearing their third (yellow/blue) kit, as seen at Villa Park? Surely not because of a clash with the officials?” – Aristos Galatopoulos

“Re Saka and rice not being rested: this is an away game at Napoli in the Champions League, with tough games to come. It’s not the Milk Cup against Oxford Utd. You still need to have a real team - points now mean rest is more likely later, when it’s more needed. And that means you simply cannot play both Gyökeres and Madueke. And Rice … well. He plays. Bruno might be a bit annoyed to be a NPC though” – Josh Hardie
There’s a long way to go. So many matches to be played. And it’s a big old table. But here it is anyway.

Arsenal’s performance was more dogged than free-flowing. But they were much the better side, dominating possession and territory, with the lion’s share of the chances. And though some wasteful finishing threatened to spoil all of their hard work, when they finally broke through it was a peach from their captain Martin Odegaard, back to his best. Another assist for Christos Tzolis too. Napoli by contrast have now lost three games on the bounce, their new boss Massimiliano Allegri already under a bit of pressure.
Arsenal start with a deserved victory.
90 min +3: Arsenal have the ball in the net again, Tzolis shooting from an angle on the left, Milinković-Savić spilling into the path of Havertz, who can’t miss. But Havertz was offside.

90 min +2: Now Neres whacks the ball away in frustration, but he’s not booked, the referee having missed it. Gabriel is furious, and runs the risk of picking up a card himself by telling it as he sees it.
90 min +1: Odegaard is booked for lashing a dead ball away, with Napoli preparing to take a quick free kick deep in their own territory.
90 min: There will be four additional minutes.

89 min: Neres pings a cute pass down the inside-left channel, and suddenly De Bruyne is free, on the corner of the six-yard box. De Bruyne has only Raya to beat, but rolls a ball across the face of goal, hoping to find Lucca instead. Lucca’s not there. The crowd groan again, at the latest of De Bruyne’s egregious errors. It’s not been a banner evening for one of the genuine greats of the last decade.
88 min: … Napoli counter, but Neres can’t get on the end of a pass down the middle. Arsenal were light at the back.
87 min: A corner for Arsenal on the right. Madueke wanders in and aims for the top left. The shot is deflected wide left for another corner, from which …
86 min: Lucca is booked for knocking into Gabriel.

85 min: Gilmour is robbed by Zubimendi and sends Guimarães away on the counter. Guimarães slips in Madueke to his right. Madueke is clear! But he can’t slip the ball under Milinković-Savić, who blocks, then spins up and stops Madueke rolling into the empty net. Madueke instead cuts back for Tzolis, whose drive hits the nearest defender. Not sure how Napoli kept that out, but they collectively managed it.
84 min: Favasuli tries to take on Hincapie in a footrace down the right, but the defender’s letting nobody past.
82 min: Guimarães looks for the top-left corner from 25 yards. High and wide. Before Milinković-Savić restarts the game, Zubimendi comes on for White.

80 min: Lucca barrels after a long punt down the middle, but can’t get the ball under control. On the touchline, Massimiliano Allegri, staring down the barrel of a third consecutive defeat so early in his reign, rants and raves in the classic continental style.
78 min: That’s now four assists in five games for Tzolis. Arsenal fans are in great voice, the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona otherwise quiet.
77 min: Napoli respond with a double change, replacing Hojlund and Lobotka with Neres and Lucca.

Arsenal get patient … and get their reward. Some metronomic passing, then suddenly a shift through the gears, as White and Tzolis combine crisply down the inside-right, cutting back for Odegaard, who pearls a rising shot across Milinković-Savić, off the left-hand post and in! What a strike!
73 min: Gyökeres and Saka, who have both been ineffective this evening, make way for Madueke and Havertz.
72 min: This game has become scrappy, and it’s probably doing Napoli more of a favour.

70 min: Tzolis meets a ball dropping towards the Napoli penalty spot … and nearly launches his shot into orbit. In terms of slapstick and comedic timing, it was almost perfect. In footballing terms, not so much.
68 min: The pace drops. It is warm in Naples after all, 27 degrees centigrade at kick-off according to Uefa’s official thermometer.
66 min: A double change for Arsenal as Merino and Eze make way for Guimarães and Tzolis.

65 min: De Bruyne, under no pressure, butchers a simple pass meant for Lobotka, in acres on the right flank. The crowd groan as the ball sails into the stand. The veteran midfielder has had a bit of a shocker so far.
63 min: Rice makes himself a little bit of time and space to the right of the Napoli D, then lashes a wild shot high and well wide right.

62 min: Hojlund strides down the left but can’t get past Gabriel as he reaches the edge of the box. His shot is deflected, and De Bryune chases after the loose ball, but he doesn’t have the legs to get past Hincapie.
61 min: Vergara also wastes little time in getting involved … but upon tearing down the left, he ruins it all by yanking a dismal cross straight into the arms of Raya.

60 min: The newly arrived Favasuli comes sliding in on Merino at 101 miles per hour. He times his tackle perfectly – just – and the crowd enjoyed that very much. A nanosecond one way or the other, though, and the Napoli sub would have been in a world of bother. He was fully committed, put it that way.

58 min: Santos left White in the dust there, such a cheeky and skilful run, but looks to have injured himself in the process. He departs, along with Politano, the pair replaced by Favasuli and Vergara.

56 min: Santos knocks the ball past White down the left and rounds the defender, then tears away. Lovely play. He shuttles the ball infield for De Bruyne, who looks for Hojlund but his radar is wonky. That’s not his first misplaced pass of the evening, and the home crowd aren’t 100 percent happy with him.
55 min: Rice clumsily clanks into Santos, and pressure that had been building for several minutes is suddenly released. Napoli so grateful for the breather.
53 min: Arsenal are pushing Napoli back. The hosts can’t get out. There’s no option for them other than long to Hojlund. The nearly-all-reds well on top.
52 min: Odegaard, dictating the tempo now from a deep position, loops another pass into the Napoli box. Again for White, but this time down the left, and not so elegant as before. Goal kick.

50 min: Odegaard suddenly springs into action, elegantly wedging a pass down the inside-right channel and into the box for White, who heads across the face of goal. Hincapie should ram home from close range, but somehow manages to leather the ball over the bar. Not for the first time tonight we say: Arsenal should be leading.
49 min: To a chorus of impatient whistling, Arsenal stroke the ball around, this way and that, 30 yards from the Napoli goal. There’s no way through the defence.

47 min: Milinković-Savić has got the mother of all hipster’s beards. He looks like he should be behind the counter at a record store, or running a micro-brewery. While he finds his feet at one end of the park, Napoli make good down the other, and Gilmour takes a whack from distance. Easy for Raya.

Napoli get the second half started. Milinković-Savić has replaced Meret in their goal. “As Big Ron used to say, ‘If you look good, you play good’,” begins Alan Baverstock. “Well, Arsenal are looking crap in all red with white sleeves once again, as anyone would, so don’t expect too much. So close, yet so far from Bill Shankly’s switch to all red at Liverpool: ‘The players looked like giants,’ he said, ‘And we played like giants.’”
Half-time fag break postbag ... which for some reason is tobacco-infused.

“Well, sir, can they boogie without the Great Scott? Presumably Mr McT is in the stand somewhere, a crafty fag on the go, cupped between thumb and index finger and held behind the back, just in case the cameras spot him” – Justin Kavanagh
“Just checking: Gyökeres is still there, right? He hasn’t gone for a lie down or some mid-half snus?” – Adam Walker

“I understand that winning games builds psychological momentum, but I feel that Arteta could use some of these essentially meaningless league phase matches to give his most overworked players the night off. Does Rice need to be on the field? Yeah, if you want to maximise your chances of winning this game. But given how exhausted he looked at the end of last season, it might be good to rest him” – Kári Tulinius

“Can you put that photo of Kai Havertz back up? At least then Arsenal fans will have a useful striker to look at. And it’d be no more immoble than the one on the pitch” – Charles Anaki [Click here to relive some of that Hot Havertz Action]
Half-time ad break. Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!
It’s been good, but not great.

45 min +2: Saka goes long. There’s a bit of pinball, before Hincapie tries to catch Meret out with a cheeky threaded shot towards the bottom left. There’s no pace on the shot, and it’s easy for the keeper.
45 min +1: The first of two additional minutes, and Konsa’s sheer determination down the right wins Arsenal a corner. Just enough time to take it!

45 min: Arsenal should be leading. Odegaard slides a pass down the inside-right channel to release Saka into the Napoli box. Saka is one on one with Meret, and looks for the top left, but gets it all wrong, the ball sailing miles off target to the left. The offside flag pops up to momentarily save Saka’s blushes … but replays show he was comfortably onside. That’s a huge opportunity passed up.

43 min: The free kick, then. A big faff, and a big waste. But Arsenal come again, Odegaard curling in from the left. Meret, who looks fit and healthy to the naked and untrained eye, punches clear acrobatically.

42 min: This game has slipped into Basketball Mode. Saka with a dribble down the right. His cutback for Rice is intercepted. Olivera probes down the left but can’t get past Konsa. Eze scampers up the other end, and is skittled by Gilmour, who goes into the book. A free kick 30 yards out, just to the left of centre.

40 min: Olivera swats Saka off the ball and sends Santos off on a wild run down the left. Santos nearly gets the better of Konsa … but the Arsenal defender somehow sticks to his side like glue, and eventually does some swatting of his own. Santos goes over, and wants a free kick, but he’s not getting one.
39 min: Politano’s in-swinging shot from the right flies straight at Raya. Arsenal counter, and Saka hoicks a dreadful effort miles over the bar.
38 min: … though having said that, Napoli’s back-up keeper Milinković-Savić is furiously prepping in the dugout. Meret puts his boot through a clearance, meanwhile, so perhaps all’s well. Let’s see.
37 min: Meret is fine to continue, and restarts the game. Everyone refreshed.
36 min: The game doesn’t restart immediately, because Meret has a problem. On come the physio. Everyone else takes the opportunity to snorkel some isotonic treats.
35 min: Rice buys a ticket from 25 yards. High and wide.

items.titleEn: Ødegaard ‘edge’ delights Arteta as Arsenal secure narrow win at Napoli
items.summaryEn: After their record-breaking feats last year in the Champions League, Arsenal are at it again. But having been delayed along with hundreds of travelling supporters by travel chaos on Tuesday, Mikel Arteta’s side had to bide their time against Napoli until Martin Ødegaard continued his rich vein of goalscoring with the crucial strike 15 minutes from full time.Perhaps it was the fact that, at Uefa’s insistence, they were forced to wear red shorts for the first time since a Premier League game against Watford in 2022 that Arsenal were not quite at their flowing best here and missed a hatful of chances. Continue reading...
bodyEn: After their record-breaking feats last year in the Champions League, Arsenal are at it again. But having been delayed along with hundreds of travelling supporters by travel chaos on Tuesday, Mikel Arteta’s side had to bide their time against Napoli until Martin Ødegaard continued his rich vein of goalscoring with the crucial strike 15 minutes from full time.

Perhaps it was the fact that, at Uefa’s insistence, they were forced to wear red shorts for the first time since a Premier League game against Watford in 2022 that Arsenal were not quite at their flowing best here and missed a hatful of chances.
Yet they were deserved winners in the end and the substitute Noni Madueke should have made the ­victory more comprehensive late on.

Having come so close to breaking their duck in this competition last year after becoming the first team to win all eight of their league stage matches, Arsenal look capable of going one better this time if Ødegaard can keep up this sparkling form.

He now has four goals in his last five games after scoring once in all competitions last year and it was the Norway captain whose name was being chanted by the fans who were kept behind more than an hour after the final whistle.

“That’s what we need – players with that mindset to decide the game and to play with that personality,” said Arteta. “He’s getting into those positions much more in recent games and I feel he has this emotional state that he knows that the ball can go in. He’s got that edge and he’s now got different relationships around him [in the team] as well. That helps.”

Arteta has bad memories of this stadium after being sent off in a 2-0 defeat during the Champions League group stage in 2013. But Arsenal’s most recent match here ended in victory as they qualified for the Europa League semi-finals under Unai Emery in 2019. Both clubs have been crowned domestic champions since then, with Napoli ending their 33-year wait in 2023 then doing it again two years later. Yet Champions League success has continued to elude them after finishing 30th in the league phase last season.

That was in stark contrast to Arsenal, who were unbeaten over 14 matches before falling at the final hurdle. It was telling that Arteta kept faith with four of his back five that started against Chelsea on Sunday, with Piero Hincapié replacing Riccardo Calafiori at left-back but failing to match the Italian’s finishing ability with one glaring miss. Mikel Merino, Eberechi Eze and Viktor Gyökeres also made their first starts of the season but largely disappointed, with the Sweden striker making way for Kai Havertz just before Ødegaard’s winner.

Those Arsenal supporters that did make it to southern Italy had no problem making themselves heard throughout, with plenty of empty seats in the home sections despite Max Allegri’s attempts to rally Napoli’s fans beforehand. The game quickly settled into a pattern as the visitors set up camp in Napoli’s half and the hosts attempted to hit them on the break. Kevin De Bruyne – no stranger to facing Arsenal after a decade in the sky blue of Manchester City – forced David Raya into a rare mistake after a typically driving run through the midfield but the ball was scrambled away to safety.

That came just after a spectacular overhead kick from Bukayo Saka at the other end had been saved by Alex Meret. Merino should have scored when he was set up by Eze’s clever header across the face of goal before Ben White drilled a shot straight into Meret’s grateful gloves.

Matteo Politano managed to test Raya again as Napoli continued to find gaps in Arsenal’s normally watertight defence. Saka blazed over after a brilliant through ball from Ødegaard on the stroke of half-time, with replays confirming the assistant had been wrong to raise his flag.

Meret did not return for the second half and was replaced by Vanja Milinkovic-Savic, once on Manchester United’s books. The Serbia goalkeeper was a mere spectator for a flowing Arsenal move featuring a sumptuous scooped pass into the area that ended with Hincapié missing the target after being picked out at the far post by Ben White’s header. Suddenly Napoli found themselves suffocated by a blanket of red. Allegri, who knows what it feels like to have lost in a Champions League final after suffering that fate twice in three years at Juventus, responded by switching to a back five and trying to hang on.

Arsenal’s pressure eventually told when another substitute, Christos Tzolis, exchanged passes with White and teed up Ødegaard, whose shot flew in off the post despite Milinkovic-Savic just getting his fingertips to the ball. Havertz had a goal disallowed for offside in injury time, but the mission was already complete.

items.summaryEn: Martin Odegaard's tremendous strike saw us kick off the Champions League league phase with a dominant win in Italy
bodyEn: Martin Odegaard’s rich vein of goalscoring form continued as we kicked off the Champions League campaign with an impressive victory against Napoli.

On a hot and muggy night in Naples, it was a case of persistence finally paying off as it took us 75 minutes to find the all-important goal after we had thoroughly dominated proceedings, but had been unable to get in front after numerous chances went begging.

But Odegaard did what he has been doing all season long and found a way to get on the scoresheet to make it five wins from five to start 2026/27, and take the first step towards trying to make it back to the final and attempt to get our hands on the trophy for the first time.
EARLY CHANCES
We arrived at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona full of confidence, having lost just one of our last 12 European away days, and soon set about silencing the noisy home fans.

We controlled the first half, creating numerous chances but unable to tuck one away. The first came on 12 minutes when a neat outside-of-the-boot cross by Viktor Gyokeres found Bukayo Saka, who connected with it via an overhead kick but it flew straight at Alex Meret between the hosts’ posts, denying us one of the goals of the campaign.

The tie reunited us with one of our former nemeses in Kevin De Bruyne, and he was in the thick of Napoli’s few dangerous moments in the opening 45, causing David Raya concern with a shot from range and then finding Matteo Politano who also drove the ball at our custodian from distance, but he was equal to it.

But after that it was one-way traffic as we peppered Meret’s goal. Midway through the half, a big chance went begging when Saka swung over a deep cross which Ebere Eze nodded back into the danger zone where Mikel Merino was waiting to pounce, but the Spaniard’s headed effort brought some great reactions from Meret who tipped it over.

The resulting corner eventually led to a good opportunity for Ben White, who popped up in an unnatural attacking spot on the left but produced a tame strike straight at Meret, who was then nearly being caught out by a wayward cross by Piero Hincapie which crept towards his near post, while Eze, Saka and Declan Rice all failed to hit the target.
BIG CHANCES MISSED

However in the 45th minute our endeavour seemed destined to land a deserved lead when Martin Odegaard played a perfect delicate pass into Saka’s feet, and the winger strode into the box, held off the challenge of Mathias Olivera before taking aim from 12 yards, but skied his shot over the top of the bar.

In total, we registered 13 shots in the first half, the most we’d managed on record in the first half of a Champions League away game, while only Real Madrid in 2023 had inflicted as much danger on Napoli on their own turf in the competition.
The second half brought a change of goalkeeper for us to contend with as Vanja Milinkovic-Savic replaced the injured Meret, but the barrage continued.

Within five minutes of the restart we again passed up a golden chance when, after a sustained period of pressure on the edge of the box, a scooped Odegaard pass finally unlocked the door and Saka found Hincapie inside the six-yard boxd box, but he also sent the ball over the crossbar.
THE BREAKTHROUGH

But on 75 minutes, we finally, finally got in front, and did so in style. Just as we’d done all game, we stayed true to our passing style and a fine move saw Bruno Guimaraes find White in the box, who then laid it off to Odegaard. With Napoli chasing shadows, he exchanged passes with Christos Tzolis and he thumped a clean strike in off the post from the edge of the box to score his fourth goal of the campaign.

With six minutes to go we had a brilliant chance to secure the victory when Kai Havertz surged forward on the counter and picked out Noni Madueke in space, but Milinkovic-Savic saved the one-on-one duel with his feet, before Tzolis’ shot on the rebound was blocked on the line.

In the final few seconds of stoppage time Havertz had the ball in the net when Milinkovic-Savic spilled a Tzolis effort into his path but the offside flag again delayed the celebrations, but only for another 60 seconds until the final whistle was blown as we extended our winning run in the league phase of the competition to 13 matches.
WHAT'S NEXT

After the first of four successive away games, we're back in action on Saturday night when we make the long trip to Sunderland, before we turn our attention to the Carabao Cup and a third-round tie with Ipswich Town at Portman Road on Tuesday. Then we finish off before the international break with a meeting with Brighton & Hove Albion on Saturday, September 19.

items.titleEn: Team news: Four switches for Napoli test
items.summaryEn: Find out the side that Mikel Arteta has selected for our first Champions League game of the season at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona
bodyEn: Mikel Arteta has made four changes to his side that will kick off our Champions League campaign at Napoli tonight, with Viktor Gyokeres, Ebere Eze, Piero Hincapie and Mikel Merino getting their first starts of the season.

The quartet come into our line-up following our 2-1 success against Chelsea on Sunday, with the Swedish striker getting the nod over Kai Havertz, who will hope to continue his excellent scoring start to 2026/27 from the bench.

Hincapie starts at left-back with Riccardo Calafiori dropping down to the replacements back in his homeland, while Merino is preferred to Myles Lewis-Skelly in midfield. Meanwhile, Eze comes in for Christos Tzolis, as the boss opts to rotate his side that has won all four games so far this term.

As for our opponents, Massimiliano Allegri made three alterations to his side, which allowed a two-goal lead to slip in a 3-2 defeat at Inter Milan on Saturday - their second successive defeat in Serie A.
Frank Anguissa picked up a groin injury in that game and is replaced in midfield by Kevin De Bruyne, while fellow Premier League alum Billy Gilmour is also included, with Antonio Vergara demoted.
There is also a change at left-back, with Leonardo Spinazzola dropped and Mathias Olivera taking his spot.

items.titleEn: Horseman hails 'world class' winner from Munoz
items.summaryEn: David Horseman on our 2-1 win over Napoli and Munoz's incredible winning goal
bodyEn: David Horseman described Luis Munoz's winner against Napoli as world class, as we picked up a 2-1 victory in our UEFA Youth League opener.

Munoz, aged 14 years and 263 days old, became the second-youngest scorer in Youth League history, just three days older than record holder Max Dowman, when he pinged his effort into the top corner in stoppage time.
After the match, a delighted Horseman reflected on the incredible effort: "The finish is just world class.

"On any stage, that's a goal that's fit to win any game. But we know that we're not just giving people token games. We brought a squad that we thought could win the game, and he was part of it. He come on and had the decisive moment.
"But it is a world class goal, and I don't use that word lightly; that's for sure."
Andre Harriman-Annous pounced to give us the lead on a scorching hot day in Naples, pressing well to force the error from the Napoli backline, delighting our head coach.

"While the angles weren't always quite right, we always had intent with our press and they did persist with it. Even when you can see they've got nothing left in their legs, they're still trying to do it. They're a really good group of kids who want to learn."
There were plenty of chances in the match, with Napoli having 28 shots to our 14. That meant goalkeeper Jack Porter had a busy afternoon at the Giuseppe Piccolo.
Assessing the win, David said: "It was a very tough game and a game where, if we're honest, we rode our luck at times. Jack made some brilliant saves.
"We had a few good spells in the game, but not as much as we would like. We didn't feel in control enough. But we have really good players we forced the mistake through the high press.
"Then one moment of magic from another ridiculously young player, which won the game. I've only been here a year, but over the last five years, we've had 50 of those games and lost.
"This competition is about trying to win and develop within the winning part of it. We've made a good start. We've got a really tough run of games, so we needed to get off to a quick start.
"This sets us up for the Lille game after the international break to hopefully really have a go at getting through the group stage this year."

items.summaryEn: All the details from our opening UEFA Youth League match of the season
bodyEn: Luis Munoz's stunning late strike helped us kick off our UEFA Youth League campaign with a 2-1 victory over Napoli at the Stadio Giuseppe Piccolo.
Andre Harriman-Annous tapped home after a loose pass in defence from the hosts in an action-packed first half.

We hit the bar twice through Axel Donczew and Maalik Hashi before Milton Pereyra levelled for the hosts on 58 minutes. The game looked to be ending all square before Munoz's incredible effort found the top corner from the edge of the box to secure all three points.
PORTER TO THE RESCUE
The first chance fell to Francesco De Stefano, who drove at the heart of our defence before unleashing a low drive that was well saved by Jack Porter.

The goalkeeper had to be alert once again moments later as Mohamed Mane raced through. His effort was well saved before the ball rebounded off the striker towards goal, only to be cleared off the line by Josh Ogunnaike.
Porter then made up for his own misplaced pass out from the back, which found Mane inside the box. The striker could not get past our goalkeeper, who tipped his shot wide.

We had our first chance after 17 minutes. Ogunnaike's dangerous cross from a free-kick found Brayden Clarke. The defender's header fell into the path of Emerson Nwaneri, who could only fire straight at Claudio Pugliese from close range.
HARD WORK PAYS OFF

We were growing into the game. Centre-back Elijah Upson, on UEFA Youth League debut for us, was able to drive through the Napoli midfield with ease to help create space for the front line. Maalik Hashi was able to find a pocket of space on the edge of the box to get his shot away, which went just wide of Pugliese's far post.

Our hard work paid off in the 28th minute. Good pressure from Ife Ibrahim on the goalkeeper and then Agostino Branchizio forced the defender to pass straight across his box and into the path of Harriman-Annous to tap home.
Napoli responded almost immediately through captain Pereyra, who looked certain to tap home but found Porter in the way to deny him from point-blank range.

The hosts were looking sharper after the hydration break in the Naples sun. A fine through-ball from Francisco Barido found Mykyta Melnyk, who tried to wrong-foot Porter with his shot, only to hit the post.

Porter produced his latest superb save just before half-time. A long cross found Melnyk at the back post, who set the ball back to captain Pereyra for a first-time finish that was pawed away by our goalkeeper.

There was just time for one last effort in the half for us as we rattled the crossbar after good work down the right-hand side, allowing Donczew to fire his effort off the woodwork. The rebound then fell kindly into the hands of Pugliese before referee Ante Culina blew his whistle for half-time.
NAPOLI BREAKTHROUGH

David Horseman made two subs at half-time, introducing Igor Tyjon and Saurap Sampang. Tyjon's good work helped launch a swift counter-attack, allowing Nwaneri got a shot away, but Pugliese saved well low to his right.
Sampang was immediately tested at right-back, as Napoli wing-back Christian Liccardo got beyond the youngster to square to Pereyra, who struck hard but Porter was a match to it.

Tyjon was causing all sorts of issues to the Napoli backline. The attacker, who signed for us this summer from Blackburn Rovers, jinked his way into the box and squared to the onrushing Hashi, who dug out an effort which flicked the crossbar on its way over.

Napoli had 20 shots in the first half, and they made the breakthrough 13 minutes into the second period. Liccardo was able to get away from Sampang and square for Melnyk at the back post. His effort was well blocked by Ogunnaike and fell to Theo Julienne, whose loose touch saw the ball fall to Pereyra, who fired home first time to level the match.
MAGNIFICENT MUNOZ
Our team took on an even younger look to it for the final 13 minutes, as Luis Munoz and Elyon Mbala were introduced by Horseman.
The hosts thought they had a winner with six minutes to play as Alessandro Rovetini lobbed Porter, but forward Ella Favicchio was given offside for his role in the build-up.
Substitute Rovetini was almost in again, meeting Porter on the edge of his box, but the goalkeeper just managed to block the effort as the hosts sensed a victory.
Both sides weren't content with a point and searched for a winner in six minutes of stoppage time. Munoz's dangerous cross evaded everyone as we couldn't tap home.

But we found our winner deep into stoppage time with a beauty from Munoz. Tyjon did well to win the ball back and fire out to Munoz, who became the youngest player in Youth League history last season, lashed his effort into the top corner from the angle.
Napoli almost levelled in the dying moments, but sub Chiaiese headed onto the post and wide as we picked up a huge victory on the road.
WHAT IT MEANS
Following our win in Naples, we'll be looking to continue our form and secure a top 22 finish in order to reach the knockout stages of the competition for the first time in this format.
WHAT NEXT
Our next UEFA Youth League match will be next month, when we take on French side Lille on Tuesday, October 13, at 1pm.
As for our other age groups, our under-18s are back in action on Saturday, September 12 against Crystal Palace. Our under-21s face Chelsea on the same day in Premier League 2.
LINE-UPS
Napoli: Pugliese, Branchizio, Lieto, Zappala, Liccardo (Chiaiese 83') , Chiummariello, De Stefano (Favicchio 80') , Melnyk, Barido (Riccio 55'), Milton Pereyra (Rovetini 83'), Mane (Esposito 46')
Subs not used: Spinelli, Lepre, Picardi, Chiaiese, D'Angelo, Rovetini
Arsenal: Porter, Ogunnaike, Clarke, Upson, Hamill (Sampang 46'), Julienne (Mbala 77'), Ibrahim (Murisa 67'), Hashi (Munoz 77'), Nwaneri, Harriman-Annous, Donczew (Tyjon 46')
Subs not used: Talbot, O'Neill, Maghoma, Abubakar

items.titleEn: Riccardo Calafiori named men's Player of the Month
items.summaryEn: Our full-back has made a flying start to the season with a goal and two assists
bodyEn: Riccardo Calafiori has been named our men's Player of the Month for August after a fantastic start to the 2026/27 season.
The Italian provided a goal contribution in each of our first three games of the campaign with a goal and two assists, as well as helping us to keep clean sheets in all three matches.
It was a lightning quick start to the new season for Riccardo, as he scored just 23 seconds into the Community Shield against Manchester City, which we went on to win 3-0 in Cardiff.

We followed that up with another 3-0 win in our Premier League opener against Championship champions Coventry City, and this time our no.33 provided the assist for the opening goal, setting up Kai Havertz to score the first goal of the new season.

Ten days later, we rounded off our perfect month with another three points and another clean sheet with a 1-0 win over Aston Villa, and once again our Italian was involved in the crucial moment, setting up Bukayo Saka to score the winner.
Riccardo won August's award with a dominant 74% of the vote, winning out over Martin Odegaard, Bukayo Saka and Gabriel.

items.titleEn: Go Inside Training before trip to Naples
items.summaryEn: We face the Italian side in our first Champions League game of the season

items.titleEn: Revitalised Ødegaard’s forward thinking gives Arsenal new lines of attack
items.summaryEn: Midfielder has been pivotal to the champions’ rampant start, becoming a potent threat with his runs into the boxAs Christos Tzolis cut in from the left flank and drove towards the penalty area, Kai Havertz could see history repeating itself.Tzolis had done just the same on his competitive debut for Arsenal against Manchester City in the Community Shield a few weeks earlier, running at his opposition full-back, cutting inside and driving at goal, before fizzing a ball towards the penalty spot. bodyEn: As Christos Tzolis cut in from the left flank and drove towards the penalty area, Kai Havertz could see history repeating itself.

Tzolis had done just the same on his competitive debut for Arsenal against Manchester City in the Community Shield a few weeks earlier, running at his opposition full-back, cutting inside and driving at goal, before fizzing a ball towards the penalty spot.

Martin Ødegaard was the grateful recipient, arriving just behind Havertz to take the ball smoothly into his path. He then faked a shot to send Gianluigi Donnarumma the wrong way before passing into the empty net.
With the scores level early in the second half of Arsenal’s win against Chelsea on Sunday, Tzolis did something very similar.

This time, his pass was intended for Havertz, but it was played ever so slightly behind the German. But Havertz had watched this before. He knew that Ødegaard, upon seeing Tzolis cut in, would have tiptoed into the penalty area.

Havertz produced a moment of genius to turn Tzolis’s slightly misplaced pass into a perfect assist, lifting his foot over the ball to leave it for his captain. Ødegaard again took the ball under his control with one touch, before this time lifting it over Emiliano Martínez to put Arsenal into a lead they would not surrender.
Ødegaard getting into more advanced positions has been an early theme of this season. He has three goals in four appearances, after scoring once in 36 outings last season.

There has clearly been an effort from Mikel Arteta and his staff to get their fit-again midfielder into attacking areas more consistently. In Premier League games this season, Ødegaard is making 3.2 high-intensity runs per 90 minutes into the opposition’s box while Arsenal have possession, up from 1.4 per 90 last term.
It’s only a small sample size from this season, but the fact that his numbers have more than doubled makes it significant nonetheless. And most important, his goal threat has clearly skyrocketed.

Similarly, he has made seven off-ball runs to make himself a cross option for a teammate in three Premier League games, almost matching his tally from last season (10). On a per-90 basis, that’s 0.65 to 2.8, or more than a fourfold increase. One of those runs led to his goal in the season opener against Coventry.

After an injury-disrupted couple of years, it appears the far-from-linear rise of the 27-year-old has taken a steep, upward turn for the better. And, for an Arsenal team looking imperious this season, that is a very positive sign.

Their captain played his part in their 2025-26 title triumph, but he probably feels more driven than most at the club to repeat the trick. He missed a big chunk of the season with a series of recurring knee injuries, and when he was available he was used sparingly.

He played 1,371 of a possible 3,420 minutes in the league – a scratch over 40.0% – and although he was available for the run-in, playing in key games and in Arsenal’s run to the Champions League final, he was a long way from the key man he has been since his permanent move to the club in the summer of 2021.

Back then Arsenal were signing a hugely talented No 10, but Ødegaard has developed into more of a No 8, a rounded midfielder who drops deep to get on the ball in front of the opposition’s midfield and moves it around the pitch.

The evidence this season suggests that we should expect to see him getting closer to Havertz more often (while also continuing to do the job of a No 8). Havertz isn’t the most reliable goalscorer, but he is an excellent and intelligent centre-forward who performs more of a false 9 role, and he needs more runners ahead of him than Viktor Gyökeres.

It appears this season that Arteta is going to prefer using Havertz up front, which will increase the need for Ødegaard to score more consistently. After the Norwegian’s start, he should at the very least challenge his season-best 15 goals in all competitions from 2022-23. He is averaging 5.6 high-intensity runs ahead of the ball per 90 this season, up from 3.9 last term.

He seems to have benefited from this summer’s World Cup, where he played a key role in his team’s run to the quarter-finals. Only Michael Olise (seven) got more assists at the tournament than Ødegaard (four).

There is pressure on him at club level, though. Eberechi Eze is breathing down his neck after standing in for him for large swathes of last season, though Arteta clearly prefers Ødegaard in the middle, perhaps for his defensive work, positioning and ability to coach Arsenal’s press on the pitch.
But there is just as much pressure on him to stay fit. He started 32, 37 and 35 of a possible 38 Premier League games in his first three full seasons, but has managed 26 then 16 in the past two.
He needs to prove he can stay fit, because not only are Arsenal better with him, but he is more likely to maintain his best form that way.

Ødegaard is showing his best in the early part of 2026-27. He is, along with Chelsea’s Morgan Rogers, one of only two players with at least 1.0 expected goals and 1.0 expected assists in the Premier League, highlighting his all-round attacking game.

Only seven players have played a role in more open-play shot-ending sequences than him (20), and he leads the Premier League for the number of such sequences where he took the shot and was involved in the buildup (four).

It helps that Arsenal look a very functional team, and have benefited from limited changes in personnel over the summer. But how much is that functionality a cause of Ødegaard’s form and how much is it a result? During his time at the club Arsenal have mounted sustained challenges for the Premier League title, and that is surely no coincidence.
Ødegaard is looking back to his best and then some, and that is ominous news for the rest of the Premier League.

bodyEn: Arsenal’s preparations for their opening Champions League game against Napoli have been disrupted after they were caught up in the travel chaos that affected airports across the UK.

Mikel Arteta was forced to cancel his pre-match press conference at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona on Tuesday after Arsenal’s flight was severely delayed by an air-traffic control issue. The Arsenal manager and his players are understood to have remained at the club’s training ground in Hertfordshire as they waited for the delay to pass after completing their morning session as usual.

Club sources have insisted there has been no alteration to their planned schedule other than arriving later than expected to the team hotel. Uefa has also agreed to allow Arsenal to cancel their mandatory press conference due to the delays, which have also affected supporters travelling to Italy for the match.

Jurriën Timber is set to be part of the Arsenal squad for the first time since the Champions League final defeat by Paris Saint-Germain on 30 May after recovering from a groin injury. The Netherlands defender missed the World Cup due to the problem that has dogged him since March but Arteta said before Sunday’s win over Chelsea that Timber was close to returning.
Cristhian Mosquera is still absent with a muscle issue but Marli Salmon, the 17-year-old defender who signed his first professional deal last month, is also part of the 23-man squad.

Arsenal won all eight of their group stage matches in the Champions League last season on their way to the final and have only lost one in their last 12 away games in the competition. But as they prepare for one of Europe’s most intimidating atmospheres, Arteta insisted they must take one game at a time despite starting the season with a 100% record in the Premier League.
“That puts us in a really good situation. The energy and the confidence around the team is high – now we have to show that,” he said.
“I’ve been in that stadium before, I know the atmosphere they create. The record at home is really, really strong. We know the challenge ahead. We are prepared and we’re ready to go.”

Napoli finished as runners up behind Inter in Serie A last season, but have made a poor start this season under their new manager, Massimiliano Allegri. Kevin De Bruyne is expected to feature against Arsenal but they are without Scott McTominay, who had a successful surgical procedure to treat an irregular heartbeat yesterday. The 29-year-old is expected to resume training in two weeks.

Napoli are also are likely to be without influential former Fulham midfielder André-Frank Zambo Anguissa as Allegri takes charge of his first Champions League match for four years. “People in this town have passion for the team, we have to start winning games again,” Allegri said. “We know we are challenging a very strong team – Arteta has done extraordinary things. Let’s face it with pride and desire.”

bodyEn: The concourses are silent when, deep in the Emirates Stadium’s bowels, Chief Inspector Pete Dearden’s briefing begins. Arsenal’s 4.30pm kick-off against Chelsea is still hours away but the fixture carries significance as a London derby and because the Premier League champions are hosting a realistic challenger.

Dearden is a senior officer in the Metropolitan police’s public order command and Sunday’s matchday commander. He is, to borrow football jargon, giving the pre-match team talk, running through intelligence and in-game tactics. “Set the right style and tone,” he says. After Dearden has finished, the police room becomes a pseudo-station for the afternoon, with all incidents triaged by the same crime officer. Football offences can be found in niche legislation, and the Met wants London’s matchdays to be, so far as possible, policed uniformly.

Matchday is the iceberg’s tip. The Met’s 17 dedicated football officers (DFOs) each work full-time on one club, planning each fixture with the matchday commander. All 500-plus games the Met covers per season are risk-graded using factors such as risk level of supporters, proximity, recent history and kick‑off time. Dearden labels Sunday’s game “medium medium”.

“Our mantra is safety, security and service,” Dearden says. “We appreciate that with 60,000 people in the stadium not everybody is going to behave, but we want to reduce the overall risk of the likelihood of disorder.”

Three police support units (PSUs), each containing an inspector, three sergeants and about 21 constables, have been assigned to the match. In addition, there are the senior team and 20 operational football officers, or “spotters”, on duty.

Clubs also have their own in-house safety teams, with, in effect, both parties doing their homework before collaborating. Arsenal’s operation involves about 1,000 stewards and response team members. They are the first responders to any incidents within Arsenal’s footprint. When a Chelsea fan overzealously reacts to his team’s early lead, the response team remove him.

Stadiums are not policed as standard, but clubs can request (and, if the request is accepted, pay for) special police services (SPS). Arsenal asked for one PSU to work within the Emirates for Chelsea’s visit but even then, police intervene only when required. Dearden estimates policing football costs the Met £23m a season, with approximately 10% recovered from clubs for SPS.

The Met is looking to close that gap, with aspects such as road closures and hostile vehicle mitigation now managed, and financed, by clubs. Dearden says his department is looking at “mitigation measures to reduce risk, which means that we don’t have to have as many police resources and we don’t compromise safety and security”.

Using spotters is one such measure. They work under the DFOs, are usually locally based for their day-to-day duties and operate consistently with one club. Dearden estimates that their expertise allows them to do the work of double the number of public order officers that would otherwise be needed. “They will go to pubs in the wider footprint where these people gather and try to identify what their plans are, get a good feeling for their mood and the numbers,” Dearden says.

Some Chelsea spotters are in Holborn and will follow when supporters journey to Arsenal by tube. Fans being unwilling to engage with spotters may indicate they are planning something. “You can get a good idea of whether they are potentially going to cause problems at a game because of that lack of engagement,” Dearden says. “It’s that communication approach again – even with some of the supporters that cause us problems, albeit a minority, there’s still engagement to be had. There are still opportunities to say: ‘Don’t do that.’”
Immediately before the match one spotter performed CPR on a supporter. The intervention was life-saving.

Outside the Emirates, two blue vans contain officers monitoring the data from cameras scanning passersby as part of an intelligence‑led live facial recognition pilot. The trials were funded thanks to a multimillion-pound Premier League investment.

Passing the cameras is voluntary, with signs alerting pedestrians to their presence. Faces are biometrically scanned and compared with a watchlist containing the several thousand people subject to football banning orders (FBOs) and individuals wanted for more serious crimes.

“We are targeting high-harm offenders, sex offenders, those with FBOs, who, if they came to an event, could spoil it for others, commit crimes, or exploit opportunities such as crowded spaces,” Dearden says.

The two-hour pilot yields six interventions, one while Guardian Sport is present. Officers intervene to speak to the individual, who is with their family. They have an FBO, although are not restricted from being around the Emirates. They have also recently been released from prison for human trafficking and are wearing a tag.
Dearden feels half a dozen hits is proportional to what would be expected. “What we can’t measure is the deterrent effect,” he says.

Noticeable is the relative lack of police visibility compared with recent years. That is by design, not accident. A heavy police presence does not necessarily make an event feel safe. “We don’t work on a ‘just in case’ basis these days,” Dearden says. “We deal with known knowns.” Arsenal fans in Naples on Wednesday are likely to meet a vastly different approach.

Immediately before the match, the Guardian laps the ground with the day’s three-person violence against women and girls (VAWG) team. “We want to change the culture of what perhaps in the past was tolerated,” Dearden says, giving the example of staff being targeted with misogynistic abuse.

“We’ve had people at football matches come forward and say: ‘I’ve heard you talk three or four times now and I’m now confident enough to report that I think I’m a victim of domestic abuse and controlling behaviour.’”
The VAWG team are also watching for those who may target vulnerable individuals.

For the match, Dearden heads to the command room with Arsenal’s safety team and the other emergency services. Proximity and open dialogue are vital. Because of the game’s risk level, there is a bronze commander, Inspector Rachel Duckett, at ground level. A half-time briefing allows all parties – including medical, the London fire brigade, the local authority, the Premier League, and British transport police – to compare notes and address issues. Dearden and Duckett then discuss the strategy for the game’s end.

For all the planning, much of what happens at football is result-driven. With Arsenal 2-1 up and time running out, a late Chelsea equaliser might have changed the mood. Home and away fans cross paths after, outside the 3,000-strong Chelsea end, where there is no cordon. Arsenal supporters gloat; some Chelsea fans react. A pair of Chelsea content creators try to record in the middle of the departing crowd and receive an expletive-laden reaction from passing Arsenal fans. They are advised to move on for their own safety.

Striking is the speed at which potential flashpoints are spotted and then defused. Officers are calm, not confrontational, and act as an external subconscious: “‘C’mon, think – do you really want to do that?’”

An hour after the final whistle, the stadium is silent again, and Dearden and his senior team debrief pitchside. A dozen incidents occurred around the game, with two arrests made – one for assaulting a steward and another for racial abuse and assault. A further 10 people were reported for offences including drinking in view of the pitch, missile throwing, low-level assault of a steward, homophobic chanting and possession of drugs.

Dearden says the number is “slightly higher than we’d like” but points out that it demonstrates proactivity. For example, stewards are told not to tolerate pushes as simply part of the job. Outcomes will be proportionate and consistency is key. In the days and weeks ahead, everything will be analysed, assessed, fed into data. Incremental improvement will be sought and further action may be required for the reported incidents.
But, for a few hours at least, all involved can reflect on a matchday’s work completed well.
